title: The Solid State of Matter
lead: A solid may hold its particles in a definite repeating pattern or in no pattern at all, and crystalline solids divide into ionic, metallic, covalent network and molecular solids by the forces that hold their particles together. Those forces explain the properties of each kind, and defects interrupt a crystal’s pattern.
objectives: Define and describe the bonding and properties of ionic, molecular, metallic, and covalent network crystalline solids
Describe the main types of crystalline solids: ionic solids, metallic solids, covalent network solids, and molecular solids
Explain the ways in which crystal defects can occur in a solid
summary_html: Some substances form crystalline solids consisting of particles in a very organized structure; others form amorphous (noncrystalline) solids with an internal structure that is not ordered. The main types of crystalline solids are ionic solids, metallic solids, covalent network solids, and molecular solids. The properties of the different kinds of crystalline solids are due to the types of particles of which they consist, the arrangements of the particles, and the strengths of the attractions between them. Because their particles experience identical attractions, crystalline solids have distinct melting temperatures; the particles in amorphous solids experience a range of interactions, so they soften gradually and melt over a range of temperatures. Some crystalline solids have defects in the definite repeating pattern of their particles. These defects (which include vacancies, atoms or ions not in the regular positions, and impurities) change physical properties such as electrical conductivity, which is exploited in the silicon crystals used to manufacture computer chips.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 10.37) The entities of a solid phase may be arranged in a regular, repeating pattern (crystalline solids) or randomly (amorphous). (Figure 10.38) (a) Silicon dioxide, SiO2, is abundant in nature as one of several crystalline forms of the mineral quartz. (b) Rapid cooling of molten SiO2 yields an amorphous solid known as “fused silica”.

(Figure 10.39) Sodium chloride is an ionic solid. (Figure 10.40) Copper is a metallic solid. (Figure 10.41) A covalent crystal contains a three-dimensional network of covalent bonds, as illustrated by the structures of diamond, silicon dioxide, silicon carbide, and graphite. Graphite is an exceptional example, composed of planar sheets of covalent crystals that are held together in layers by noncovalent forces. Unlike typical covalent solids, graphite is very soft and electrically conductive. (Figure 10.42) Carbon dioxide (CO2) consists of small, nonpolar molecules and forms a molecular solid with a melting point of −78 °C. Iodine (I2) consists of larger, nonpolar molecules and forms a molecular solid that melts at 114 °C.
Graphene sheets can be formed into buckyballs, nanotubes, and stacked layers.
Types of crystal defects include vacancies, interstitial atoms, and substitutions impurities.

exercises.prompt: What types of liquids typically form amorphous solids?

answer.solution: Liquids made of large molecules, or of a mixture of molecules whose movements are restricted, typically form amorphous solids. As such a liquid cools, its bulky molecules cannot move into a definite repeating pattern before they are held in place, so it freezes with its particles randomly arranged. Candle wax is an example: it is composed of large hydrocarbon molecules and solidifies as an amorphous solid. Fast cooling has the same effect on a liquid that could otherwise crystallize: molten silicon dioxide cooled rapidly gives the amorphous solid fused silica instead of crystalline quartz. Metals and ionic compounds, whose particles are small and move freely in the liquid, typically form ordered, crystalline solids.

exercises.prompt:
As it cools, olive oil slowly solidifies and forms a solid over a range of temperatures. Which best describes the solid?
(a) ionic
(b) covalent network
(c) metallic
(d) amorphous
(e) molecular crystals

answer.solution: (d) amorphous. A crystalline solid has a precise melting temperature because every unit in it is held by the same forces, so all of its attractions form and break at one temperature. Olive oil instead solidifies over a range of temperatures, which is the behavior of an amorphous solid. Its molecules are large and of several kinds, so they are structurally nonequivalent: some attractions are weaker than others, and they take hold at different temperatures as the oil cools, just as they break one after another when an amorphous solid is heated and softens gradually. Ionic, covalent network, metallic, and molecular crystals all have a definite melting temperature, so none of them fits.

exercises.prompt: Explain why ice, which is a crystalline solid, has a melting temperature of 0 °C, whereas butter, which is an amorphous solid, softens over a range of temperatures.

answer.solution: Ice has a crystalline structure stabilized by hydrogen bonding. These intermolecular forces are of comparable strength and thus require the same amount of energy to overcome. As a result, ice melts at a single temperature and not over a range of temperatures. The various, very large molecules that compose butter experience varied van der Waals attractions of various strengths that are overcome at various temperatures, and so the melting process occurs over a wide temperature range.

exercises.prompt:
Identify the type of crystalline solid (metallic, network covalent, ionic, or molecular) formed by each of the following substances:
(a) SiO2
(b) KCl
(c) Cu
(d) CO2
(e) C (diamond)
(f) BaSO4
(g) NH3
(h) NH4F
(i) C2H5OH

answer.solution: (a) SiO<sub>2</sub>: covalent network, one of the compounds whose atoms are joined by an unbroken network of covalent bonds. (b) KCl: ionic, a metal with a nonmetal, built of K<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions. (c) Cu: metallic, copper atoms held by metallic bonding. (d) CO<sub>2</sub>: molecular, discrete CO<sub>2</sub> molecules held by IMFs. (e) C (diamond): covalent network, each carbon atom covalently bonded to its neighbors throughout the crystal. (f) BaSO<sub>4</sub>: ionic, built of Ba<sup>2+</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> ions. (g) NH<sub>3</sub>: molecular, discrete polar NH<sub>3</sub> molecules held by IMFs. (h) NH<sub>4</sub>F: ionic, built of NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> and F<sup>−</sup> ions even though it contains no metal. (i) C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH: molecular, discrete ethanol molecules held by IMFs.

exercises.prompt:
Classify each substance in the table as either a metallic, ionic, molecular, or covalent network solid:
SubstanceAppearanceMelting PointElectrical ConductivitySolubility in Water
Xlustrous, malleable1500 °Chighinsoluble
Ysoft, yellow113 °Cnoneinsoluble
Zhard, white800 °Conly if melted/dissolvedsoluble

answer.solution: X is metallic, Y is molecular, and Z is ionic. X is lustrous and malleable and conducts electricity well, the properties Table 10.4 gives for metallic solids, whose atoms sit in a sea of delocalized electrons; its melting point of 1500 °C is typical of a transition metal, and metals do not dissolve in water. Y is soft, does not conduct, and melts at only 113 °C, so its particles are neutral molecules held by weak IMFs; these properties match sulfur. Z is hard, melts at a high 800 °C, dissolves in water, and conducts only when melted or dissolved, which is the behavior of an ionic solid: its ions are held in place in the crystal and become free to move only in the liquid or in solution.

exercises.prompt:
Identify the following substances as ionic, metallic, covalent network, or molecular solids:
Substance A is malleable, ductile, conducts electricity well, and has a melting point of 1135 °C. Substance B is brittle, does not conduct electricity as a solid but does when molten, and has a melting point of 2072 °C. Substance C is very hard, does not conduct electricity, and has a melting point of 3440 °C. Substance D is soft, does not conduct electricity, and has a melting point of 185 °C.

answer.solution: A is metallic, B is ionic, C is covalent network, and D is molecular. A is malleable and ductile and conducts electricity well, properties found only in metallic solids, and its melting point of 1135 °C is typical of a transition metal. B is brittle and conducts only when molten, because its ions become free to move in the liquid; its melting point of 2072 °C is the very high melting point of an ionic solid such as Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. C is very hard, does not conduct, and melts at 3440 °C, the properties of a covalent network solid, whose melting requires breaking covalent bonds, as in diamond. D is soft, does not conduct, and melts at only 185 °C, so it is built of molecules held by IMFs; table sugar is a molecular solid with this melting point.

exercises.prompt:
Substance B is hard, does not conduct electricity, and melts at 1200 °C. Substance B is likely a(n):
(a) ionic solid
(b) metallic solid
(c) molecular solid
(d) covalent network solid

answer.solution: (d) covalent network solid. Hardness, no electrical conductivity, and a high melting point of 1200 °C are the properties Table 10.4 lists for a covalent network solid, whose atoms are held by a network of strong covalent bonds. A metallic solid would conduct electricity well, and a molecular solid would have a low melting point, so neither fits. An ionic solid is also hard with a high melting point, but it conducts electricity when molten or dissolved because its ions become free to move. Substance B is described as not conducting at all, so the covalent network solid is the likely choice.
